slides.headline: Both sides hurt. That changes the differential.
slides.body: Most pain has one origin: how this person walks, sits, swings, sleeps. When the same picture shows up on both sides at the same time, load alone has a hard time explaining it.

slides.headline: Bilateral symptoms widen the picture.
slides.body: One-sided pain usually traces to load history. When both sides match each other in tempo, location, and intensity, the cause is likely living above the muscle layer.

slides.headline: Three differentials live behind a bilateral picture.
slides.body: Compensatory loading can mirror across symmetric athletes (lifters, runners, cyclists). Spinal-origin pain refers bilaterally when central or bilateral nerve roots are involved. Rheumatic disease is systemic by design and shows up symmetric.
slides.goldAccent: One side narrows the search. Two sides opens it.

slides.headline: Screen before you treat.
slides.body: When the pain is bilateral and matches across both sides, I run the rheumatic and neurologic screens before touching tissue. If the screens are clean, we treat the load story. If they flag, the patient sees the right doctor first.
slides.quoteText: Both sides matching is data. It tells me to look at the system or the spine before I look at the muscles.

slides.headline: Same complaint, three different roads.
slides.body: A bilateral compensatory pattern still gets PT first. A rheumatic flag means rheumatology and bloodwork before progressive loading. A central spinal flag means an imaging conversation with the medical team. Same complaint, three different roads.
slides.goldAccent: Treating the wrong category wastes months.

slides.headline: Your threshold is higher than they told you.
slides.body: If both knees, both shoulders, or both hips keep flaring at the same time and one provider keeps treating one side, send me a DM and let's read the pattern.
slides.tagline: Be Good. Help Someone. Learn Lots.

caption:
Both sides hurt. Both knees. Both shoulders. Both hips. That changes the differential.

When pain shows up on one side, the cause is usually load history: how you walk, sit, swing, sleep. When the same picture shows up bilaterally, load alone has a hard time explaining it.

Three differentials live behind a bilateral picture. Compensatory loading can mirror across symmetric athletes (lifters, runners, cyclists). Spinal-origin pain refers bilaterally when central or bilateral nerve roots are involved. Rheumatic disease is systemic by design and shows up symmetric.

So when bilateral symptoms walk in, I run the rheumatic and neurologic screens before I touch tissue. If those are clean, we treat the load story. If they flag, the patient sees the right doctor first.

Same complaint, three different roads.

If both sides keep flaring at the same time and one provider keeps treating one side, send me a DM and let's read the pattern.

Be Good. Help Someone. Learn Lots.
